newsitem.title: USA: House panel approves $13 billion interior spending.
newsitem.headline: House panel approves $13 billion interior spending.

text.p: The House Interior appropriations subcommittee Tuesday approved a $13 billion spending bill for land and energy programs in fiscal 1998.

The spending level was $100 million less than the Clinton administration requested and $500 million less than was approved for 1997, but 1997 funding included more than $600 million in emergency spending.
The two most controversial provisions would exclude $700 million for land acquisitions approved in the White House's budget agreement with Congress and shut down the National Endowment for the Arts.

Of the $700 million the White House wanted to buy land, $65 million was intended to pay off a company to stop the planned development of a gold mine on the edge of Yellowstone National Park and $250 million was to buy back forest land to protect Headwaters Forest in northern California.

Subcommittee chairman Rep. Ralph Regula, an Ohio Republican, said that while lawmakers might favor the plans to protect Yellowstone and Headwaters House committees in charge of authorizing the plans had not approved them yet.

He said he did not want to spend the rest of the $700 million on land acquisitions, the only purpose for which the money was approved in the budget agreement. "In Indian health and education the need for facilities is enormous. Yet none of the $700 million could be used for it," he added.
The panel rejected an amendment by Rep. David Obey, the top Democrat on the House Appropriations Committee, to include $65 million to block development of the mine near Yellowstone.
Obey, from Wisconsin, said the panel had to be bound by the budget agreement. "We have no ability to make policy judgments in the national interests of the country," he said.

The subcommittee also rejected a Democratic amendment to save the National Endowment for the Arts, but Regula said he expected the House to vote on the issue and seek funds for the sometimes controversial agency that provides grants for arts programs around the country.
The Senate was also expected to support continued funding of the agency, which meant the issue would have to be resolved when the House and Senate put their spending bills together.

The subcommittee approved $1.2 billion for operating the National Parks, up $78 million from this year, and included a provision that would allow the parks to keep about $130 million in fees they collect. In previous years, parks fees went straight to the Treasury and were not necessarily used to pay for parks maintenance, a system that gave parks little incentive to collect fees.
The bill provided $1.3 billion for the National Forest System and called for the federal government to sell 3.8 billion board feet of timber in the 1998 fiscal year, which begins on Oct. 1.
The bill also called for the government to sell $209 million worth of oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve to cover the costs of running the reserve.
